Ἐὰν ταπεινώσῃς σαυτὸν, ὑπομένῃς τὰ συμβεβηκότα, παῤῥησιασθήσῃ ἐνώπιον

πράξει διαμονὴν, ὥστε σε λαμπρὰς καὶ ἐπιδόξους ἔχειν τὰς πράξεις. ΚΕΦ. ΚΓʹ. Στίχ.

λέγειν. Ὁρᾷς πῶς ἐπέτυχεν ὅπερ ηὔχετο; Τοῦτο γὰρ ἔσχατον γέγονεν ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ.
Ἤθελον μαθεῖν τί μοι ἤμελλεν ἐρεῖν, καὶ εἰ ἔμελλέ μοι ὁμοίως κο λάζειν. Ταῦτα δὲ
εἶπον, οὐχ ὡς καταγινώσκων ἀδι κίαν. ΚΕΦ. Κ∆ʹ. Στίχ. ʹ. Ἡδύνθη αὐτῶν ἄρτος εἰς
νεωτέ ρους. Ἡδὺ, φησὶ, τοῖς ἀσεβέσι τὸ τρέφειν νεανίσκους, ἐφ' ᾧ δύνασθαι δι'
αὐτῶν τὰς ἐπηρείας ἐργάζε σθαι. ΚΕΦ. ΚΖʹ. Στίχ. βʹ. Ζῇ Κύριος, ὃς οὕτω με ἔκρινε.
Ἔλαβεν ἐξουσίαν τοῦ Ἰὼβ ὁ διάβολος, καὶ ἤτασεν αὐτὸν νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας,

pass_a_gloss: …of works. That is, the being filled of houses with good things. Verse 19. But a blameless one sneered at them. At whom? Or the counsel of the impious? For instance: they want to teach someone things opposite to the truth, in saying; the things they say, having wicked doctrines. Seeing these things the blameless one sneers. Verse 20. And fire will devour their remnant. Of the same. This which has been left among the impious, the former ones having died, the fire will devour. Verse 22. And he took a declaration from his mouth. The declaration, I was seeking by myself, what it signifies. And I found in another edition in place of it confession. He says then rather: confess about your sins; take from the mouth of God a declaration with confession; and take up his words from your heart. These things Eliphaz was saying, admonishing, as he supposed, Job. Verse 23. But if you turn and humble yourself before the Lord. He admonishes him toward turning, supposing him to have suffered these things having sinned. Verse 24. And as a rock of a torrent of Sophir. From the place where the gold comes into being it will come upon you; as it were, your word will be varied and beautiful. Verse 25. The Almighty then will be to you a helper from enemies. If you subject yourself, if you confess. Verse 25. And he will render you pure like silver fired. A healthy doctrine (gap in the print) fired, God. Verse 26. Then you will speak freely before the Lord. Of the same. If you humble yourself, endure the things that have happened, you will speak freely before the Lord, you will have freedom of speech, as having put off the sins. Verse 28. Upon your ways there will be light. Of the same. If you keep admonition from me, and turn and confess. These things then were being said toward Job; but not justly were they said; for he did not sin. But if it is said toward us, it is said justly. Verse 28. And he will restore to you a way of life of righteousness. And to say simply: all, he says, the continuance fitting to a righteous doing for you, so that you have your doings bright and glorious. Chapter 23, verse 2. His hand has become heavy upon my groan. But if it were possible, he says, on the spot to bring the vote of the punishments, it was possible to find him. Would that it were possible to go to law, he says, and to meet him, and to learn what were the things which he was going to say to me toward these things which I was going to say. Do you see how he attained the very thing he was praying? For this has come to be last in the book. I wanted to learn what he was going to say to me, and whether he was going to punish me likewise. These things I said, not as condemning injustice. Chapter 24, verse 6 (label as printed). Their bread was sweetened toward younger ones. Sweet, he says, to the impious is the feeding of young men, so as to be able through them to work the insults. Chapter 27, verse 2. The Lord lives, who thus judged me. The devil received authority of Job, and examined him night and day, first through the outward things, later through the body itself, after these also through the friends. For when he tested it through the wife, and Job has not been conquered, the devil brought three friends, not enemies, not having plotting doctrines, but words of truth, but not well, nor in season brought forward. And the devil was planning through these friends to make Job utter something against the Providence, to be impious through the toils, to lose heart through the pains. But the truly courageous one, the enduring one, see what he says after the words of the three. When Eliphaz completed three discourses, Sophar two discourses; for these having been completed, those having fallen silent, see what he answers after the preamble spoken by him, thus named by the Scripture. What does he answer? Let us attend to the wording. Verse 1. And Job, adding further, said in the preamble: Verse 2. The Lord lives, who has thus judged me, and the Almighty, the one who embittered my soul, and the things following. I know from where…
pass_b_english: … works: that is, to have houses filled with good things.

“But the blameless man sneered at them” (Job 22:19). At whom? Or is it at the counsel of the ungodly? For example: people want to teach someone things that are contrary to the truth, by what they say, holding wicked doctrines as they do. When the blameless man sees these things, he sneers at them.
“And fire will devour what is left of them” (Job 22:20).
From the same: Whatever has been left behind among the ungodly, once the earlier ones have died, the fire will devour.

“And receive a declaration from his mouth” (Job 22:22). I kept asking myself what “declaration” means. And in another edition I found “confession” in its place. So he is really saying: Confess your sins; receive from the mouth of God a declaration together with confession, and take up his words out of your heart. Eliphaz said this to admonish Job, as he supposed.
“But if you turn and humble yourself before the Lord” (Job 22:23). He admonishes him to turn, because he thinks Job has suffered these things for having sinned.
“And like a rock of the torrent of Sophir” (Job 22:24). From the place where gold is produced it will come to you; that is, your speech will be rich and beautiful.
“So the Almighty will be your helper against enemies” (Job 22:25): if you submit yourself, if you confess.
“And he will render you pure, like silver refined in the fire” (Job 22:25). A sound doctrine … refined in the fire: God.
“Then you will speak freely before the Lord” (Job 22:26).
From the same: If you humble yourself and endure what has befallen you, you will speak freely before the Lord. You will have freedom of speech, as one who has put away his sins.
“There will be light upon your ways” (Job 22:28).

From the same: If you keep the admonition I give you, and turn, and confess. These things, then, were said to Job; but they were not said justly, for he had not sinned. If they are said to us, however, they are said justly.

“And he will restore to you a righteous way of life” (Job 22:28). To put it simply: he will give you back, he says, the whole settled state that suits a righteous life, so that your deeds are bright and glorious.

“His hand has become heavy upon my groaning” (Job 23:2). If it were possible, he says, to have the verdict on these punishments given on the spot, I could find him. Would that I could go to law, he says, and meet him, and learn what he would say to me in reply to what I meant to say. Do you see how he obtained the very thing he prayed for? For this is what happened at the end of the book. I wanted to learn, he says, what he would say to me, and whether he meant to go on punishing me in the same way. I said these things not as one who charges him with injustice.
“Their bread has become sweet to the young” (Job 24:5). The ungodly, he says, find it sweet to feed young men, so that they can carry out their outrages through them.

“The Lord lives, who has judged me thus” (Job 27:2). The devil received authority over Job and examined him night and day: first through the things outside him, later through his very body, and after that through his friends as well. For when he had tried it through the wife and Job was not defeated, the devil brought on three friends. They were not enemies, nor did they hold treacherous doctrines; they spoke words of truth, but not well and not in season. And through these friends the devil planned to make Job utter something against Providence, to turn ungodly because of his toils, and to lose heart because of his pains. But look at what the truly brave man, the man of endurance, says after the speeches of the three. Eliphaz had finished three speeches and Sophar two. When they had finished and fallen silent, look at what he answers after the preamble he spoke, as Scripture itself names it. What does he answer? Let us attend to the wording.
“And Job went on and said in his preamble” (Job 27:1): “The Lord lives, who has judged me thus, and the Almighty, who has embittered my soul” (Job 27:2), and so on. I know from where …

choices.issue: Third person in the old English
choices.choice: The Greek is first person (ἐζήτουν κατ' ἐμαυτὸν ... εὗρον ἐν ἄλλῃ ἐκδόσει): rendered 'I kept asking myself ... I found in another edition'.
Rendered as the lead-in 'From the same:' opening its own paragraph; the attribution is not extended or guessed.
'Chapter 23:', 'Chapter 24:', 'Chapter 27:' removed; the catena labels appear only as KJV references after each lemma.
'Ὑγιὲς δόγμα ...... πεπυρωμένον, ὁ Θεός' kept with its gap: 'A sound doctrine … refined in the fire: God.' No connecting words supplied.
φησί kept as 'he says'; the paraphrase in Job's first person ('I wanted to learn ... I said these things') kept first person.
Opens mid-sentence ('… works') and ends mid-sentence ('I know from where …'), as the locked Greek does.
Kept the Greek forms 'Sophir' (place, LXX 22:24) and 'Sophar' (the friend), as the text spells them.
